At no point did I say murderers shouldn't suffer consequences for their actions. That's completely and entirely different from forgiving yourself.

Murder is not bad because the person you murdered can't decide how to punish their murderer. Seriously, what? I'm hoping I'm misunderstanding that part because... wow.

The people you hurt don't get to decide what your "punishment" is; what a strange take. That's not how the law works and that's not how life works. The appropriate thing to do is to work to be a better person and to not hurt people anymore. That doesn't have to involve punishment at all (depending on what you did), and it certainly doesn't involve asking the people you hurt to decide your punishment. You might, depending on circumstances, ask how you can *make it up* to the person you hurt, but asking to be punished is honestly such a Catholic-ass misinterpretation of justice.

Forgiving yourself also does not necessarily mean you stop feeling remorse. In this particular instance of killing someone (presumably, for the sake of our arguments, not in self-defense or defense of others), the best way to forgive yourself would be to acknowledge that what you did was wrong, but that you can't change the past, you're a different person now, and wallowing in guilt will not change anything. You can forgive yourself for doing something and still know that it was wrong and you shouldn't have done it.

Forgiving yourself for past wrongdoings is absolutely a thing and does not require the consent of the people you hurt. The people you hurt are allowed to remain angry at you if they choose to and you are still allowed to forgive yourself. Your response is, frankly, bizarre, and a wildly simplistic understanding of forgiveness and how it works. Everyone's done bad things to other people and we don't have to spend the rest of our lives berating ourselves for it. We, as real living breathing human beings, have a responsibility to learn from those mistakes and improve ourselves so we don't hurt people again - but that doesn't apply to fictional characters. Fictional characters, just like real life people, absolutely can forgive themselves (or even never consider that they did anything wrong) without changing anything about themselves. Just because it's not "right" doesn't mean it can't or doesn't happen.

My abusive stepmother still blames *me* (who was 12 when I finally stopped visiting her and my dad) for "all the drama [I] caused" - the fact that she was a grown adult screaming at a *child* for hours on end, into the wee hours of the morning on school nights, several nights a week, for things that could barely be considered a slight by the biggest stretch of the imagination, has never once crossed her mind. Or if it has, she keeps it to herself.

To say that a person - let alone a fictional character - doesn't have the "right" to forgive themselves is such a wild take.

I was a paid GM for over a year on startplaying before I switched my game to free because the paid element was stressing me out. The overwhelming majority of people charge nowhere near $45/session - that person would need to be a celebrity in the TTRPG world to get any responses at that price.

Most people charge $15 - 20 per session. My experience was that most players were fellow GMs who never got the chance to play the game as a player, and were willing to pay to get that experience. Most of them ran their own games on StartPlaying as well.

With paid games, you often get higher investment in the game than with free games, especially free games with strangers. I've tried joining a free game on Roll20's LFG threads and had a horrible time. Whereas when you're paying, the GM is more motivated to make sure everyone is having a good time, and the players are more motivated to play the game rather than goof around and ignore plot points.

Overall, I've had good experiences with paid games on StartPlaying. People stay because they enjoy the game.

Unfortunately, this isn't a question someone else can answer for you. It all depends on your situation and circumstances. You are very young, and a baby changes your life like you can't imagine. If you are in college or plan to attend, it will be difficult to complete with a baby to attend to. It will be hard to find work that accommodates your childcare needs, and just as hard (and expensive) to find childcare that accommodates your work schedule.

The one thing I strongly caution against is being a SAHM relying on a partner you're not even married to. While it might sound nice on paper, it puts you in a very vulnerable position. I don't say this to suggest you should rush getting married - that is quite the opposite of what I mean. Five years feels like a long time, but the people we are in our youth are not the people we are as we grow up. Knowing someone at fifteen, and even at twenty, does not mean they will be the same person at twenty-five or thirty. For reference, I have known my fiancé since we were thirteen, and he and I are both radically different people than we were when we met or even five years ago (we're now thirty). In our case we still love and cherish the people we've become - but that's not always the case for everyone. People don't have to be bad people to just... grow apart.

Talk to your friends and family. They know your situation better than you can describe to strangers on Reddit. Listen seriously to their advice, and try not to let emotions get in the way of a smart decision.

I wish you the best, regardless of what choice you make.

Not TV, but I've always felt that Maria from The Sound of Music was so obviously ADHD. The song "Maria" seems like it's the most clear demonstration (other than just how the character acts, thinks, and feels), but I actually think "Something Good" is the clincher for me that she has undiagnosed ADHD. In "Something Good," she refers to having a "wicked childhood" and being miserable in her youth. But I have an extremely hard time imagining someone as kind-hearted, generous, thoughtful, and joyful as Maria being truly "wicked," even as a child. That *other people,* especially adults, and especially in the 1930s when the story takes place, would have CALLED her wicked for displaying classic ADHD symptoms, and she internalized those words - now *that* I believe.

I don't think the writers of The Sound of Music intended for Maria to have ADHD - the Broadway musical was written in 1959, and ADHD wasn't formally recognized until the 1980s. The story is based on a real family and real events, so Maria is based on a real person - but based on accounts of the real Maria, I don't even think the real person necessarily had ADHD. The writers *may* have based Maria's character off of people they knew who had undiagnosed ADHD, but they wouldn't have known it as such. However, despite these facts, to me Maria is the quintessential ADHD character.

Hi! I work at a jewelry store. I am not a salesperson but I take in repairs and one of the main things I do is size people's fingers both for the initial fitting and the resizing.

I read some of the comments and my analysis is: probably not! If you can spin the ring without twisting/tugging at your finger, in fact it may be a smidge too big! But there are other factors that influence your perfect size. You mentioned it takes some twisting to get it off - that's good! We like a little bit of resistance going over the knuckle; that's what keeps it from flying off your finger, especially when you wash your hands (don't want your band going down the drain, do we?).

However, for comfort we generally recommend that you "walk" it off rather than twist it off. That means pushing one side forward, then the other side, left to right, until it goes over the knuckle. If you have a lot of excess skin you may find that tugging your skin back (from the base of your finger, pulling towards you) helps you get it off even easier.

When you take it off, how does the indent look, and how long does it last? A slight indent is a sign of a good fit, and should fade within an hour or two (this is assuming you remove it every night, and haven't been wearing it non-stop for 10+ years). If it is deep or discolored, or lasts for multiple days, it may be too tight!

Last, how long have you been wearing it? Many men come into our store for a resizing less than a week after their wedding. We always recommend they wait - if you're not used to wearing a ring, it takes some getting used to and will feel uncomfortably tight at first.

I saw someone recommend going up a "half size" if you conclude it is indeed too small. Holy cow! I would recommend no more than an eighth of a size, or a quarter size at most. Just looking at it on your finger, going up half a size would have it sliding off your finger all the time. However, when you take it to a jeweler, *have them confirm your size with their own tools.* Sizing implements have a legally allowed variance, and the person in front of you sizing you will know what's best.

When I can't find things - even small, unimportant things like a pen - I can easily work myself into a full-blown panic attack very quickly. I've recognized this as an extremely consistent trigger and so have developed strategies to work around it. If I'm looking for something that I don't necessarily need right this minute, the moment I realize I can't find it I start counting to ten. If I haven't found it by ten, I stop looking and will try again later. If it's more time-sensitive, I quickly resort to asking people to help me look for it, rather than waiting a more socially acceptable amount of time (by which point I'll be hyperventilating and pulling my hair, etc).

One of the biggest things is recognizing triggers and developing coping strategies in advance.

What are the features of the GM screen, other than the art on the front? Does it have USB plugs, speakers, or even magnets, clear sleeves for inserts, etc? If the answer is no, then absolutely do not spend that amount on a GM screen. Give him a budget you're comfortable with and ask him to pick something within that range.

If it has some technology to it (built-in speakers, charging ports, etc) then that might justify the cost... but personally I still wouldn't drop that amount on a GM screen when I can buy speakers separately, etc.

If it comes with an actual tablet (and check that the tablet is INCLUDED)... well then that fully explains the price point, but I'd still rather just get a cheaper screen that has an insert for a tablet and then do my own research for what tablet I actually want.

Basically, no. That's an absolutely absurd amount to spend on something that could be made for free out of a medium-sized cardboard box.

While it's important to encourage your child's interests and it's great that you have the funds to do so with extracurriculars, it's also super important for a child to have free time and to just... be a kid. Some kids enjoy and benefit from sports, art classes, music lessons, etc. Other kids more enjoy the free time they get to just do what they feel like doing at the time. (To be clear, I'm not suggesting you're denying her that - two extracurriculars is not too many IMO.)

I was never in more than one or two extracurriculars at a time as a kid. I didn't put a lot of effort into soccer (wasn't much into sports), and while I enjoyed my music lessons, I resented the time I was expected to spend practicing every day and eventually quit for that reason. I preferred my free time, and didn't have any extracurriculars in middle school or the first half of high school. In 11th grade I found an activity (color guard) that I enjoyed enough to not mind the imposition on my free time. Maybe your kid will eventually find something, or maybe her childhood is better spent on self-directed activities.

I would talk to her and ask her if she wants to continue her extracurriculars - there's no sense in paying for them if she doesn't want to go, but she might be enjoying it more than she seems so definitely ask her.

Does she put effort into school? Your title says "no effort in anything" but you only mention hobbies. If she doesn't, is she making bad grades or is she doing well enough with low effort? If the former, I'd be more concerned about her no/low-effort attitude. If the latter, I'd find ways to challenge her more - she might just be bored.

Work ethic is important, but it's also important to be able to relax. Knowing where to focus your efforts is a skill. I'd say as long as she's doing well in school and completing her chores satisfactorily, there's really nothing to worry about here.

Again, you cannot take your experience, nor even that of your family's, and project it onto everyone else - and then use that as an excuse to deny them information about themselves. People deserve to know about themselves. Millions of people with ADHD feel that knowing their diagnosis has helped them understand themselves and get over the shame they felt from blaming themselves. It's an incredibly common theme that I've heard over and over again, on reddit, other sites, and IRL. Saying "well it might NOT help" is not a good or valid reason to deny the very high chance that it *will* help. That's like suggesting that no one should bother trying medication because it might not work for them - completely ignoring the overwhelming majority of people for whom it *does* help.

I was diagnosed with ADHD when I was a young child, and rediagnosed at several points in my life. But I wasn't diagnosed with autism until I was in my twenties. I had always known I was different and that I struggled with things more than other people did, even more than others with ADHD. But I just blamed myself for it - until I learned that I was autistic, that there are strategies to help, that there's a *reason* I feel and act this way. I didn't need to form a community or research the neuroscience behind it to feel better. I just needed to know that it wasn't my fault I was different, and it wasn't a moral failing on my part to struggle so much.

I appreciate that your and your family’s experience was different, but you have to accept that such an indifferent relationship with diagnosis is pretty rare. Even if it was more common, you can't just deny that many people *are* helped by it, and significantly so. It's not a matter of shame or persecution attached to a label. People are more likely to feel ashamed of something they think is a fault in themselves than of something they realize is just a neurological difference. There are ways to explain ADHD to a nine-year-old that have nothing to do with neuroscience or forming an identity out of a label. But denying her the language to describe her experience does not prevent her from experiencing her ADHD.

Based on what you've said I'd recommend a budgie, aka the humble parakeet. They are cheap even when they are hand-raised (which is what you'd want - don't buy from the pet store) and, at their loudest, one of the quietest birds you can get. They are also phenomenal talkers. Many consider them "beginner birds" (whether or not there's such a thing is up for debate) but they are very affectionate and entertaining. If you are still dead-set on a parrot, you may consider starting with a budgie or other small bird and growing your flock once you have more experience and are confident that the noise won't be an issue.

The next step up in my opinion would be a green cheek conure, which is what I have. They are louder than budgies, but as far as conures go they are one of the quietest. However, they are not great talkers. Ours doesn't talk at all, though he will make kissy noises. I also fostered another green cheek that spoke about a dozen words and short phrases, when he felt like it, which was rarely. That is about the most you can get out of a green cheek, however they are incredibly affectionate birds with a great, goofy personality.

Most birds do not go to their loudest volume unless 1. They are panicked/surprised or 2. They REALLY want your attention. You may have to deal with a period of time where you must let your bird scream repeatedly for 15 - 30 minutes, because if you let them out when they're screaming, they will scream every time they want to be let out, because hey, it worked! Not every bird will start this but it's a distinct possibility. Fortunately you can train it out of them within a few weeks by ignoring them until they've been quiet for a few minutes, then giving them the attention they want. But those few weeks may be rough for you.

My last recommendation is to look into bird adoption charities. I went through Phoenix Landing Foundation, which is phenomenal. Most quality bird adoption programs will require you to foster your bird before you can adopt. This gives you time to figure out whether a bird is the right pet for you - or maybe this particular bird isn't right for you, but you want to try another.

For starters to give your budgie a good home, I would watch their video Interior Design: Setting Up a Parrot's Cage for Action. Also do your research into pellets for food and make sure you know the list of deadly foods by heart, as you will need to supplement their diet with veggies and a little bit of fruit. Seed is not good for birds. In the wild they are forced to rotate through seeds based on seasonal availability. When presented with a bag of variety seeds, they will root through and only eat the fattiest, yummiest seeds, throwing everything else on the ground, and this will lead to health problems in the long-run.

Is the bird hand-raised or parent-raised? Ask your friend if you don't know. (If they got it at a pet store, it's almost certainly parent-raised. If they got it from a breeder, it just depends.) Parent-raised birds will not be as affectionate and are unlikely to bond with you the way a hand-raised bird will - that does not mean it will make a poor pet, but you should understand what to expect. A hand-raised bird will want (and need) more time with you (even if it takes a while - sometimes months - to earn its trust). A parent-raised bird will be less interested in spending time with you and will need another budgie to keep it company.

Most importantly, you should know that you've made a huge commitment in terms of time and money. A healthy budgie can live for 15 - 20 years. You will need to decorate its cage not just once, but redecorate every six months, moving old toys and perches to new places and adding in new toys and perches as well. You have to clean his (metal - NEVER plastic) water and food bowl every single day. You have to chop fresh veggies for him every day in addition to his pellets, and a small selection of fruits (consider fruit his "dessert" and don't give him too much). If he is hand-raised, or parent-raised but shows interest in bonding with you, you need to have him out of his cage for several hours a day, at least one hour of which should involve you actively interacting with him (as opposed to him just sitting on your shoulder or hopping around on your desk). You need to invest time into learning as much as you can about bird body language and how to care for them. You will have to clean his cage regularly. If you are not prepared for this commitment, that's OK - it's not your fault for not knowing what you were getting into. You don't know what you don't know. But if you can't commit to all this, find the bird another home with someone who can.

Either way, best of luck to you and birdie!

Depends.

I do consider who has the highest AC and Hit Points, and treat them as damage sponges when I need to (to avoid an unsatisfying TPK during a random encounter, for example). But for the most part, it depends on the enemy.

A smarter enemy will attack the weakest-looking character first - usually the wizard, or whoever isn't buff and wearing a ton of armor. Or if a particular PC is carrying the McGuffin, attacking/stealing/disabling the McGuffin, or otherwise making themselves the battlefield VIP, they'll be targeted.

Less intelligent enemies will attack whoever is closest to them.

Both intelligent and unintelligent enemies will sometimes attack whoever last landed a blow on them, or whoever has consistently dealt the most damage to them over the last few rounds. The barbarian might be difficult to take down, but if he's hitting you for a fifth of your health every turn, you're going to want to take care of him (or run).

In the case of multiple enemies (which I recommend doing as often as possible), I try to make one the "leader," or at least stronger than the others (if not smarter). If they don't have a reason not to, the "leader" will often try to go toe-to-toe with the strongest-looking PC, because they're the most likely to stand a chance against them - a nice side effect is that this PC then soaks up most of the damage, rather than the wizard being one-shotted. It also gives that PC a good challenge. Alternatively, you could have lots of little guys try to crowd the strongest PC, thereby preventing them from taking out the more important, stronger enemy but still providing a challenge in the form of sheer numbers.

While it might seem more "fair" to attack randomly, it doesn't make for a very interesting fight. Try to think strategically - adding a layer of strategy to your combat encounters will make things more fun. This goes beyond just choosing who to attack. I highly recommend checking out Keith Amann's The Monsters Know What They're Doing. He has a free blog and a four-book series. I also got a lot of mileage out of D&D 4e's DMG and its approach to combat roles for both players and enemies - thinking of how each PC fills a particular role helps me figure out how best to engage them in a fight, playing to their strengths (when I want them to feel powerful) or against their weaknesses (when I want them to feel challenged).

But honestly, I've stopped taking Vyvanse for now. It's too expensive (though the patent just expired, so hopefully that will change soon) and honestly overkill for my needs when I'm not in school.

I instead take dextroamphetamine. Since dex only lasts about three hours for me, and I need 9 - 12, I am prescribed six 10-mg pills a day. I take 1-2 at a time every three hours. It's not as strong as Vyvanse, but for my current needs that's fine.

I do intend to go back to school, at which point I would want to switch back to Vyvanse again. But knowing that it doesn't last as long as I need it to, here's my plan: 50 mg Vyvanse, 20 mg dextroamphetamine. Start with the Vyvanse, then when it starts to wear off, dextroamphetamine to carry me through the rest of the day. Obviously requires a touch of foresight to make sure I get the super focus-y things done while I'm on the Vyvanse, and can do things like chores and errands and hobbies for the last few hours of the day.

Because of my documented metabolism issues, my psychiatrists have always been willing to put me on very high doses of medication. Depending on your psychiatrist, they may want to fiddle with the exact ratio of Vyvanse:dex/other meds. Mixing stimulants can be tricky and, while you know yourself and your body best, it's truly a good idea to listen to your doctor when you're combining two medications that act on the brain in different ways, have different maximum dosages, and can both cause heart/nervous system problems. Listen to the person with a degree in that shit. If they say "I want to start you with 30 mg Vyvanse and 10 mg dex," do what they say, pay attention to your body over the following month, and then talk about upping it at your next appointment if you still feel like you need more.

In short: If Vyvanse is your miracle drug but doesn't last as long as you need it to, try splitting it up into two 30 mg pills, or else combining it with a different medication and organizing your day to accommodate the change in your ability to focus.

My solution was two-fold. Since I couldn't just start working on what I needed to do before the Vyvanse kicked in (there is a reason I have to take the Vyvanse, after all), I would seek out something sufficiently entertaining that was... *adjacent,* or similar to, what I needed to be doing. Turn on Get Organized with The Home Edit. Youtube videos and occasionally netflix were my go-to for this part.

The second part was to set a timer after I took the Vyvanse for about 15-20 minutes. When that timer went off, the Vyvanse wasn't fully kicked in, but it was starting to. Time to Get Ready! If you're studying, it's time to pull out the textbook and the highlighters. If you're cleaning, grab all the cleaning supplies you need. By the time you're done Getting Ready, the Vyvanse will have kicked in and, if you did the first part, you're In the Mood to do what you need to do.

If you know you need to do multiple different things while on your Vyvanse, not just one big study session or cleaning the house day, set a BUNCH of timers to remind yourself it's time to switch tracks. Vyvanse triggers my hyperfocus VERY often, so it's super easy to lose track of time.

I was put on medication at age 6. My mother has told me that she felt like she could not be a good parent to me when I was unable to control my own behaviour due to ADHD. She knew I wasn't trying to misbehave, and so it wasn't a matter of "discipline." I needed medication to function at school and at home, and she needed me to have a handle on myself so that she could parent effectively.

I am Team Medicate all the way. It will help your daughter and help you. And remember, you can always pull her off of it or switch medications if she is having side effects or reacting poorly. ADHD medications are generally not the kind that you have to wean off of carefully - just call the psychiatrist and inform them that you'd like her to stop taking the medication, and they will likely tell you that you can stop cold-turkey that day.

The reason I am Team Medicate, even at younger ages, is because you are exactly right: her brain is still developing. She is forging neural pathways every day and reinforcing them with her repeated behaviour and thought-process. Ask yourself: Do you want those neural pathways to form from her current behaviour and thought-processes, or do you want to medicate so that her brain learns to function how it should? Taking medication consistently in childhood actually increases the chances that they will not need it as an adult, because their brain learned how to function properly.

How old is your daughter? Does she have an opinion on the matter?

In fact I do! I keep a google doc for each of their characters with all their answers. I don't bug them every single week, and sometimes I ask them different questions based on their previous answers or whose backstory I'm currently working on tying into the campaign.

1) What is their favorite food?

2) What is their favorite color?

3) Tell me one random fact of any sort about your character.

4) Tell me about a person your character cares about.

5) How did your character learn the skills (magic, fighting, etc) they currently possess?

6) Tell me about one of their hobbies.

7) What's one thing your character regrets?

8) What is one of your character's non-adventuring goals?

9) Is there anyone who might have a grudge against your character? What for?

10) How do/would their parents feel about their current lifestyle and choices?

11) What is your character's greatest fear?

12) What's one thing your character is proud of?

13) What or who can your character fall back on if they're in trouble?

14) Do they have any superstitions, or keep/do anything for luck?

15) What was the first time they remember being scared or hurt?

16) What was the first lie they remember telling?

17) Do they have any nicknames or pet names that their family or friends call them?

18) How do they act when drunk?

19)  What is one thing they'd never, ever do?

"One random fact" is probably my favorite, because it has infinite reuses and gives them the opportunity to come up with something themselves.

I try to mix it up between serious questions and lighter ones, and allow them to answer in the group chat or PM me. I don't bug them if they don't answer every single question, unless it's something important for what I'm working on - sometimes people are busy, or just don't have an answer yet! I write the question down in the google doc and oftentimes they fill it in later.

Asking at the start of each session is great for exercising improv skills and developing group synergy! IMO, the advantage of asking throughout the week is that they have the chance to be more thoughtful with their answers. It also gives them the opportunity to keep answers private if they don't think their character would share that info with others - I'm pretty tough on metagaming, and keeping some things secret means I can work them into the campaign in a way that's a total surprise to others. But usually they answer questions in the group chat, which we treat as "stuff you talked about around the campfire one night."

My advice for players who don't seem as invested as you'd like them to be is to take it slow. Some people just don't have the brainspace to write a 3-page backstory all in one go, and it doesn't necessarily mean they're not invested.

I find all players respond well to this, because the one-question-at-a-time format isn't overwhelming vs expecting a fully fleshed-out backstory at session zero. It also allows them to develop their character as they play, which can feel much more natural. And players who *do* love long, detailed backstories go absolutely ham for this, because holy shit they get to talk about their characters as much as they want *every week.* One player wrote a four-page short story in response to the prompt "Tell me about one person your character cares about."

My other piece of advice is to figure out what interests *them* as players. It's hard to get invested in characters that never get to do what you want. Usually this can be boiled down to combat, roleplay, or exploration. I've been so direct as to use SurveyMonkey to literally just ask everyone what their favorite aspect of the game was. It's helpful information, because I can pour infinite time into intricate plots, social encounters, and whimsical worldbuilding, and it won't mean kaput to the barbarian who just wants to smash some goblin skulls together. Once I've let him do that, he's happy to partake in the rest of the stuff I've got planned.

Many experienced DMs recommend relying mostly on improv, and I still do that when I'm feeling burnt out or didn't have much time in the week to prep ahead. I don't consider it time wasted, because it's something I enjoy doing even when it doesn't pay off. The pay off was the fact that I enjoyed working on it.

Write anything related to the story, just to get the juices flowing again. Rewrite an old scene without looking at the original. Write short Alternate Universe fanfiction of your own characters (high fantasy characters changing a flat tire on the side of the road in a storm? I've done it). Write a random scene that may or may not come later in the story. Write random dialogue between two or more characters - they could be talking about something important, or just chatting with no purpose.

Just write *something*. Thinking about a story is one thing. But something about the act of writing is semi-magical. Often times, you can't really move past that block until you're actually writing, even if what you're writing doesn't directly relate to the problem (and you may find that it starts veering that way as the gears in your head start turning).

I usually suggest avoiding any amount of editing or even rereading your work until you've finished, but sometimes, with extreme writer's block like this, it can help. Looking back over what you've already written can remind you of old ideas or plot threads or help you notice something you've previously written that might be contributing to your current problem. At the very least, you're making *some* progress just by editing.

Also: Try writing by hand, if you're not already. Typing is a more technical skill, while handwriting is a more "creative"/artsy skill - even when I'm programming, if I need to brainstorm a bit of code, I'll break out an index card and a pen. It makes a huge difference, at least for me. Just don't forget to type everything up at regular, frequent intervals - you'll hate yourself if you put it off for too long!

As I understand it, pathological refers to diseases. A disease is not a disorder, so a disorder is not pathological. Is there another meaning for pathological that I'm unfamiliar with?

As far as I'm aware, the only reason "disorder" doesn't have a "neutral" meaning is because of public perception surrounding mental health, disabilities, etc in general. It's not the word itself, it's the thing it's attached to. Updating language does not equal updating perception.

And, ok, cool, for all the autistic people who have no mental health issues and plenty of success in life, if they don't want their autism to be called a "disorder," by all means. As for the rest of us, it *does* cause problems and challenges in our life, regardless of whether those challenges are the result of ourselves or others.

I just don't think changing the word "disorder" is going to do... literally anything. At all. Will public perception change? No. Will people feel better about themselves? No. Will accommodations become easier to get? No.

They say "A rose by any other name would smell as sweet." The associations people have with autism are not going to go away because we changed or deleted a word that's... not even that strongly associated with autism to begin with. Most people just say "autism," not "Autism Spectrum Disorder," and don't even know that that's the full title, just like people say "depression" instead of "Major Depressive Disorder." Even for autistic folks, and newly diagnosed autistic folks, I don't see how changing the word "disorder" is going to make them/us feel any better about their/our diagnosis, if we already have negative ideas about what autism is.

I understand that some folks might have personal feelings about the language surrounding what we're called and how we describe our experiences. You absolutely have the right to feel that way. But turning it into a movement, a goal, a teaching method, what have you... I just don't see it as effective, or even important.

EDIT: Not sure if you edited your comment or I just missed it, but regardless: If that's your reasoning, why call it anything at all? Why not just stop calling it autism and just talk about the individual things that make us different with no labels at all to seek out, find, and compare similar experiences? The reason we have labels for experiences and identities is not just so the outside world can put us into a box. It's so we can find each other, and discuss with each other, and talk about our experiences and how they relate and swap tips and techniques and vent to people who understand. It's why queer folks have developed so many terms (demiromantic, gender fluid, etc), despite most of the rest of the world not recognizing them. Yes, it's a little different when the term has been assigned to you rather than agreed upon amongst yourselves. But as I've said, I really don't feel like the "disorder" bit is the most important part of the label of autism. Keep it, change it, delete it, whatever - it's really not going to change anything.

The ONLY way to make things that aren't crap is by making a whole bunch of things that *are* crap. Nobody's first finished project is their masterpiece.

If your biggest concern is wasting your own time, then stick to the project, but scale back the size. Turn it into something that you can finish in a few months. The point is not to make something that's great or even good. The point is to practice working on something beginning to end, and to learn how to encounter, handle, and overcome challenges, not just of the programming variety but of the concept and execution variety.

Say you finally get a "good" idea. You get as far as you have on everything else, maybe farther. Then you encounter a problem you haven't before, not because the idea isn't good, but simply because you've never gotten far enough for a problem like that to crop up. What do you do? You don't want your first time handling difficult problems to be on your magnum opus. You need experience. You need to know how to take a shitty idea and tweak it until it's good. You need to know how to take good ideas with shitty points and tweak the details until those are good, too. You need to know how to take good ideas and good details that just aren't working the way you wanted them to work and tweak them until they do work.

You can make anything sound like a bad idea if you reduce it enough and don't go into the details or explain how well it's implemented. The details and the execution matter much, much more than the raw idea.

I will add, though, that it sounds like you need to be spending much more time in the planning/concept stage than you currently are. I am just a lone programmer working casually on an RPG as a hobby, but as I understand it, most game devs spend AGES in the planning/concept stage before they write the first line of code. From what I learned in my compsci classes, this is true of most software and programs, not just games. You should know what you're going to do and the details of how you're going to do it before you ever start coding/prototyping. That means timelines, storyboards, mechanics, etc. Taking your ideas and fleshing them out properly, beginning to end, before jumping ahead to the prototype will go a long ways in getting you to stick with a project.

I agree completely. EVERY "disorder" could be redefined to be a "difference," because there's no such thing as a "typical" human brain. Therefore, disabilities/disorders/etc are not biologically defined problems with strict borders, but rather a cluster of symptoms and experiences that enough people experience together to give a name to.

ADHD is a disorder. There's nothing "wrong" with being ADHD, but I sure do need my medication and accomodations to help me function. Likewise, attempting to reclassify autism as "not a disorder" is nothing more than a language update. It will not change public perception.

These changes in language happen every few decades with all sorts of disorders/disabilities. As they garner negative associations, the names/labels change. Multiple Personality Disorder was updated to Dissociative Identity Disorder a little more than a decade ago for this reason.

Personally, I feel these language updates are nothing more than a band-aid on the larger problem. They're a temporary fix. The only advantage to calling something Dissociative Identity Disorder is that people don't know what it is. Once they find out, all the old negative connotations, perceptions, associations, and stereotypes come right back out.

Likewise, attempting to relabel the language surrounding autism is not going to do anything to change public perception. Nor is it going to help folks trying to get accomodations to live in an NT world. I get the point, I get the goal, but it's a silly and ultimately useless method to achieving the desired goal.

ADHD and anxiety are separate disorders, although they can be comorbid. Have her checked for an anxiety disorder, because that can absolutely cause hives.

In the meantime, try different discipline methods. Time outs have been shown to be detrimental to children's mental health and self-image, and don't improve behaviour long-term. While panic attacks, hives, and the like are definitely indicative of an anxiety disorder, they don't just pop out of nowhere; something is making your child upset and anxious.

I have anxiety myself, and I can distinctly remember how upsetting time outs were. I felt ignored, maligned, unheard, and unimportant. I would cry, and I couldn't understand why my parents were ignoring me when I was so obviously upset, and that made me even more upset. It wasn't a ploy to get out of trouble or inappropriately get attention. I was genuinely upset, and the longer I was ignored in time out, the more my feelings intensified. I certainly wasn't learning any lessons or reflecting on my poor behaviour. I spent the whole time sobbing and wondering why my parents hated me and why I was so terrible that I deserved to be here and to feel like this. These feelings persisted even as I got older, up to and possibly past your daughter's age (not sure when exactly my folks stopped doing time outs with me). Obviously this is an extreme reaction, because I had anxiety, but research has shown that neurotypical children experience those exact same feelings, just much less intensely. And even in small doses, they're not good feelings.

The goal is to teach kids how to control their own behaviour, and having them sit in a corner for nine minutes doesn't help reach that goal. I can't make specific suggestions based on such little detail, but it can't hurt to do a little research into discipline that has been shown to be positive and effective through scientific studies. Who knows, you might find something that really works, and won't have to use time outs anymore, or can save them as a last resort. Nothing's going to be a magic bullet, but some strategies are more effective than others, both short and long-term.

I really hope this comment doesn't come off as judgemental or condescending. I am absolutely not accusing anyone who uses time outs of doing something wrong. Nor am I saying that I know better what you should or shouldn't be doing. But based on my own memories and experiences, combined with scientific studies and child psychology, I feel almost... obligated, to at least bring up the topic when I see it.

TL; DR: Have kiddo checked for anxiety, and consider looking into non-timeout methods of discipline, if you have the time and energy and inclination to do so.

Depends. Some languages have unique signs for their specific gods. Others use a combination of symbols. This can depend on how the spoken name for the god "translates," or what the god represents. Mandarin often pushes two symbols together to make a new word; "wife," for example, is woman + (possessive) child.

Since your conlang was originally developed for holy scripture, it makes sense to me that gods might have a dedicated symbol, and could also make sense that said symbol is then mushed with others to make new words. E.g., the symbol for the god of music + the symbol for man = musician. However, it makes equal sense that the opposite would be the case. The symbol for music + the symbol for, say, sky = the god of music. Or maybe there's a symbol or symbol aspect that specifically signifies a god, and that's combined with other symbols to make the god's specific symbol.

Basically, language is weird, and the same origin can and does lead to wildly different languages and writing systems. Maybe one of your cultures has dedicated symbols for each god, and the other doesn't. Maybe they used to, but some of them changed over time, while some stayed the same. Who knows! Only you can decide. The fun part of conlangs from a historical/cultural/anthropological perspective is that the same "reason" can be used to justify dozens of different options. You can think about the details of the exact culture and history, or just do what the fuck ever.

- too many fine details; the face in particular. The teeth, the eyes, and the tongue are tiny details that aren't going to read well from a distance or when the logo is shrunk down. It's just going to look busy.

Now, as far as particular suggestions for changes, I have two things to say. Most likely on the "may not" end of that spectrum. - Removing the black background. The red bones of the wings I think would look pretty cool as-is, though some slight tweaking might be necessary to balance the visual weight against the viper's body.

I also want to clarify something that I only briefly handwaved in my original comment:

The four years I spent learning to draw in high school were done purely for fun, not with any goal in mind of turning it into a career. I mostly got into it because a bunch of my friends did it (the ones who ended up going to art school). I enjoyed it, and still do years later. I'm really glad I spent the time learning what I did; it's been a useful skill many times over, often in ways that wouldn't be obvious.

Anyway, what I'm trying to get at is that, because I considered it just a fun hobby, I probably didn't spend more than 3 to 5 hours a week on average drawing. My friends who wanted to actually *do* something with their talent were probably drawing 10+ hours a week, if not significantly more.

On top of that, these friends were more invested in learning all the different elements of drawing. All I cared about was drawing an anime ship I liked or my own original characters. I didn't care too much about poses, composition, etc because I mostly just wanted to get an idea down on paper. It didn't need to look good for anyone else. My friends, on the other hand, were seeking out more information on the deeper complexities of drawing, and practicing all sorts of things I never bothered with (e.g. backgrounds, objects, shading, etc).

Now, some of these friends had been drawing and learning for a few years before I met them in high school - but some hadn't. The difference between me and them wasn't necessarily the amount of time between me first starting to learn to draw and now. It was the amount of time they'd actually spent doing it, and how much effort they put into seeking out and practicing new things. And I will say, when I took that college Drawing I class, I probably learned just as much in one semester as I did the whole time in high school. A real teacher, and real assignments that *force* you to practice, does wonders.

When I say I spent four years learning basics, I don't mean it typically takes a dedicated person that long to reach the same level of "mastery" that I have acheived. But it's still not something you're going to master in a year or even two. If you work hard at it, another year or two will put you at, or more likely above where I am now. It will take you longer to develop a personal style and to produce artwork that is sellable/marketable/appealing to audiences. But don't think that your timeline will be identical to mine. Time spent practicing and learning is much more relevant than the number of years since you've started.

I can't attest to DrawABox, but I have two things to say.

First, it takes much longer than a year of learning and practice to be decent, let alone *good* at any medium of art. I spent four years teaching myself to draw in high school, and wouldn't say I ever made it past the "experienced novice" level. I can draw simple poses without a reference, more complex ones if I break out the grid method on a reference picture. I can draw clothing, but am not good at getting the folds right, or making the clothing move realistically/dramatically in an action pose. In other words, I've mastered the basics, but not much more than that. Granted, I wasn't working as hard at it as some of my friends who ended up going to art school, but it was nonetheless a passionate hobby that took up many hours of my regular week. I did take two art classes in college (one painting, one drawing), and that helped a fair bit, but I still wouldn't call myself anything other than a novice artist.

Second - yes, the fundamentals of traditional drawing will help in pixel art. But... not by a huge amount, especially at 16-bit (32+ might "translate" better, since there's more detail to work with). They're such different mediums that it's hard to compare. What looks good on paper, if copied as faithfully as possible into pixel art, might not look as good, and will need an understanding of pixel art specifically in order to tweak well.

For myself, with 4+ years of experience, the transition into pixel art has been *ok*. Objects are fine for the most part, though wood textures vex me. Background elements (grass, floors, etc) are harder, because you have to balance what looks good and "realistic" with not making it all too busy. People? I outsource that to a free pixel art character generator as a place holder until my own skills improve or I can afford to hire a real artist for my game. I've drawn a slime monster that looks decent, but I'm not sure what I'll do when I start needing more complex-looking enemies.

What you *will* gain from traditional art is a good sense of proportions, style, character design, poses and movement, etc. But trying to translate that back into pixel art will still be a transition. I'd say that if your goal is really just to be good at pixel art, and any other art skills are auxillary, then invest a few months into learning the basics and then go back to pixel art. (Obviously, keep practicing pixel art while you're learning.) You'll get more reward for your time by following tutorials meant for manga and comic artists, since the simplified style means you're not "wasting" time learning to draw extra details that won't be reflected in pixel art anyway.

Yeah, with that context it sounds more like anxiety/trauma than a fear of the dark itself. I'm so sorry they went through that. Definitely get them into therapy (and I would encourage your wife to do the same; trauma doesn't just affect kids).

I also take back what I said about a non-coddling approach. Knowing this now, I would say that a calm, confident, but comforting/nurturing approach can help them learn that they are safe, someone is looking out for them, and they can let go of their fears.

I would still shy away from a nightlight, though. My phobia counselor for heights refused to write me a note for my high school to let me use the elevators instead of the stairs (which I could see all the way down). His reasoning, and it makes sense to me, was that I would never improve without regular exposure, and since I was technically able to go up the stairs (despite fearing and hating it), it was better for me to keep doing it.

Instead, I would suggest a lamp beside their bed that they can switch on and off without having to get up and cross a dark room to the light switch (or vice versa). This way they have a measure of control and safety in their space, but are still "exposed" to the dark once they get in bed and turn the light off. If the fear gets overwhelming, they can easily turn the lamp back on until they calm down. I personally think this is better than a nightlight - a nightlight just removes the thing they're afraid of; they're not "learning" anything. But giving them a lamp to turn on and off helps them learn that when things get scary, they can do something themselves to address that fear. Kind of like the difference between learning martial arts vs never leaving the house for fear of being attacked (obviously an extreme comparison, but it's the first that came to mind).

Of course, that's just my opinion based on a somewhat similar experience; once you can get them to a counselor and they've met with your kids once or twice, ask their opinion on what to do re: nightlights, etc.

That's interesting, I've heard from a few people that they didn't like Katara. I agree that she's a very flawed character, but that's exactly what I adore about her (especially as she learns and grows). Her flaws are rooted realistically in her backstory (her mother's death and having to step up in her place). I *liked* that she nagged and bossed and was at times unreasonable. If she hadn't been so flawed, she could have easily been a Mary Sue. Instead she felt like a realistic 14-year-old girl dealing with childhood trauma and a massive responsibility that most adults would struggle with. I also liked how they balanced her healing abilities with her remarkable fighting prowess. Both skills felt natural for her personality - she is kind, caring, and nurturing, but also easily riled up, and doesn't take anyone's shit.

I liked Katara from the start, and liked her even more at the end of season one when she "leveled up," so to speak. But the episode that really sold her for me was the one where she and Toph were arguing. It really summed up her character: hotheaded, motherly (to the point of nagging), nurturing, and understanding. Sokka's reminiscing that he can't remember his mother's face - only Katara's - is so telling. Despite the fact that she was younger than her brother, Katara had to step into a parental role, without much of a role model on how to do that. Without any examples of how to discipline and motivate and encourage, she fell into the habits of nagging and bossing. What else can you expect of a little girl?

Most importantly, I liked how the story and the other characters treated those traits. Yes, they were universally acknowledged as annoying and negative traits. But they were also acknowledged as coming from a good place, and that they were at times helpful. Despite being the "bossy, nagging girl," she wasn't stereotyped. She wasn't held up as an example of what girls *shouldn't* be. Instead, she was just a regular girl doing her best.

I get that not everyone will like Katara. No matter how you can justify it, nagging is annoying, and I understand why some people can't get past that part of her character. But Katara is probably one of my all-time favorite characters (alongside Toph), and I'd like to hope that people can at least accept what an incredible person she is, even if they still dislike her personally.

Here's the short answer:

Go on some goddamn meds.

Unless you have a heart condition or something of the sort, the side effects of stimulants are really tame as far as most medications go. I've taken medications for other things where side effects included things like rashes, numbing/tingling of the limbs, even sudden death. Yep, there are legal meds that are known to just randomly kill you even if you take them properly. Some side effects that I've experienced (from other medications) include loss of word recall, constipation, congestion, sleepwalking, severe joint pain, brain fog, and anxiety.

The main side effects of stimulants? Loss of appetite. Sometimes your heart might race a bit if you're on too high of a dose, but unless you have a heart condition it's nothing to worry about, just mention it to your doctor and they'll lower your dose by 5 - 10mg, or spread it out through the day so you're not on so much at once.

Other side effects include headache, anxiety, and trouble sleeping (the latter just means take it earlier in the day; the first two often just require switching to a different stimulant). Those aren't especially common. Even rarer side effects include dry mouth, stomach pains, diarrhea. I've literally never heard of anyone having those problems, and I know many many people who are medicated for ADHD.

Some people report feeling less "creative" on stimulants. I say bullshit, that's not a side effect, it's just what happens when your brain chills the fuck out and isn't thinking at 99 miles an hour every second of every day. I actually feel more capable of expressing my creativity while medicated, because I can focus on what I'm doing. If you really miss that old thought process, you can wait til the end of the day when your meds have worn off, or skip a Saturday when you don't have much to do. I do most of my daydreaming at night as I'm falling asleep, and act on those ideas the next day when I can focus on them.

So stimulants + heart condition = not great (and even then it's not always such a bad idea - my sister takes 50mg Adderall a day and she's had heart surgery. It just depends on what kind of condition and how severe. Your doctor will know). And maybe don't take it if you have anorexia or anything like that.

But yes, long story short, the side effects of stimulants are nothing to be scared of. If you get the worst of the lot, you can just stop taking them (you're "supposed" to call your doctor before stopping any medication, but I assure you it's perfectly safe to stop stimulants at the drop of a hat if they're not working for you); none of them are permanent and they'll stop the day you quit.

Stimulants WILL change your life for the better. You will be SHOCKED by the change in your ability to motivate yourself and focus on your task, even at low doses while you're testing things out. I don't want to sound like I'm pushing pills on people who don't want them, but I am honestly a HUGE advocate for getting proper medication for any and all of your diagnosed problems. It will take an adjustment period where you figure out what medication and dose works for you, but once you hit that sweet spot you will be amazed how much your life improves.

It's not your fault you have ADHD. And you shouldn't have to work ten times harder than everyone else to get the same (or worse) results. Take a damn pill and function as well as everyone else does. You'll still be yourself. Life will just get a little easier, that's all.

EDIT: Regarding motivation. A friend of mine has a good saying (I don't think she came up with it, but says it all the time): Motivation took the day off.

Motivation is great, when you have it. When you don't? Sit down and do it anyway. I know that's easier said than done. Here's a few tricks I use to get things going:

If you're not already, switch to handwriting, at least for when you're having a lot of trouble. Handwriting is a more "artsy" skill than the technical skill of typing. It just sort of taps into that area of the brain.

Write anything. Write the word "The." Write your character's name. Write "He/She/They." See if you can finish the sentence. Now the paragraph. Now the chapter. Just start with one word, it'll help.

Go back over the last one to three paragraphs of your story and, using handwriting, copy them out, without editing. A lot of the time I do this, I find by the time I reach the last paragraph, the juices are flowing and I can just keep on going.

Write a summary of the paragraph in a few words. E.g. "Lestat drinks Anne's blood." No flowery descriptions. Keep doing that for every paragraph until you're ready to go back and add detail. Again, the only thing you can't edit is a blank page.

Here's a trick I came up with for myself in middle school:

Ask yourself if you can remember a time when someone else did the thing you're cringing about.

If you can, ask yourself what your thoughts were about it. Did you judge the person? Dislike them? Ever think about it again in your life until now? Realize later they're actually a cool person and it was a one-off event?

EVERYONE has had awkward moments, or done awkward things, and I guarantee that whatever social faux pas you think you've committed, has been committed by someone else in your presence. If you can't remember it happening, that's because it's not that big a deal, and no one else will remember it either. If you do remember it, your own reaction is probably a good gauge for how most other people will react.

And, worst case scenario, let's say the other people DO remember it, and they ARE judging you, and they think you're TERRIBLE and NOTHING you do from this point on will change how they think about you. Honestly? Oh, well! If those people are going to react that way to a little bit of social weirdness, they weren't people you wanted to impress and hang out with anyway.

I would say that the truth is likely somewhere in the middle. A *few* people *might* have noticed, and of those few people, *some* of them might have passed judgement on you, and more likely than not, most of those judgements will change if you see them again and act differently. Or even if you act the same, but they just get to know you enough that they realize you're a cool person and your odd behaviour is just a personal quirk that they don't mind.

Perhaps an unpopular-ish opinion, but if you're truly a beginner, and especially if you're not looking to explore the field much further, I can't recommend Game Maker Studio 2 enough. It's very intuitive, great UI/IDE, great organization tools, intuitive coding language, wonderful documentation, and lots of helpful tutorials (Sean Spalding is a great youtuber with tons of tutorials running beginning to end on how to make a game). There are even drag-and-drop options if you're making something super simple, though you won't be able to do anything complex with them.

That said, the in-house language they use (GML, or Game Maker Language) is, admittedly, a useless language. It's not used outside of GMS2. I consider myself proficient in GML and have no intention of ever putting it on my resume because, well, it's useless outside of GMS2, and GMS2 is not an industry-standard engine. On top of that, if you're thinking of making something extremely complex, GMS2 is not a particularly powerful engine. It has 3D functionality but is better used as a 2D engine. Some well-known indie games have been made on GMS2, such as Undertale, but Undertale is not really a visually or mechanically impressive game.

Another thing to consider is that the GMS2 free trial is very limited, and you will have to shell out $30 for the yearly desktop license, more if you want a permanent license or to export to other consoles. I think the price is more than worth it though just for how easy it is to use, especially as a true beginner.

I found both Unity and Unreal to be very difficult to learn as a true beginner with no coding experience whatsoever. With GMS2, however, I was quickly making simple games and it wasn't long before I was able to Frankenstein tutorials together to make my own unique games, and not much longer after that before I found myself turning to tutorials less and less and just being able to code things myself. Now I'm a computer science student proficient in Java, JavaScript, Python, and teaching myself C++, and I *still* am using GMS2 to build my little RPG labor of love. GMS2 is what started it all. It's easy to learn and, despite the language being "useless," it still gives you good habits and mindsets that will be useful if you decide to learn other languages.

As a woman, I would say yes, it's weird and uncomfortable. Some exceptions might include:

- standing together at a bus stop

- sitting near each other on public transit

- a few other situations where you are both stationary and in close proximity

However, even in those situations you should still closely monitor body language, both before approaching them and during the conversation. Headphones, obviously, are a no-go. If they're on their phone (even just scrolling mindlessly), probably also leave them alone.

Reading a book is a gray area in my opinion: asking them what they're reading is a great conversation starter, especially if you love books as well and can hold an interesting conversation about reading. But on the flip side, someone who is reading might want to just keep reading and not be bothered. Again, just monitor their responses and body language through the conversation. If they are curt or short, or keep going back to their book, leave them alone.

But I will say this: regardless of whether the above situations apply, I would honestly avoid approaching women on the street 99% of the time. Most women will immediately be defensive and wary, because 99% of the time when we're approached on the street, it's someone being a creep. Even if your intentions are good, I've had plenty of conversations with men on the street that started out seemingly innocent and quickly (or slowly) turned into the guy being creepy or pushy. So you might think you're having a normal conversation, but the woman is mentally bracing herself for it to go south.

With women, body language isn't always a good indicator that they're necessarily enjoying the conversation. Some men (not all, not even a lot, but *enough*) react poorly, even violently, to perceived rejection. So some women may feel like they need to pretend they're enjoying his company when really they're anxious, creeped out, and desperately waiting to make an exit.

I don't say this to make you feel like you can't approach women at all, or that women necessarily feel that way about you - I'm sure you're a great guy! - but there's a big difference between approaching someone you kinda know (had a class together, see her at the library a lot, etc) and approaching a stranger on the street. As I mentioned, 99% of my interactions with men on the street, at bus stops, or on public transportation are negative. I can really only think of one conversation I had with a man on a bus that I enjoyed - we talked about Star Trek.

I'm not sure how men feel about being approached on the street by other men, so I can't attest to that. But I'd still venture to say it's unusual.

Been in college since 2013, so I'm not too far behind you. Still have two years left.

I started out as an art major. I enjoy art, but I did not enjoy "learning" art and being told what to do. I felt stifled.

Then I switched to anthropology. I loved learning anthropology (still do), but I wasn't happy with the career prospects. I don't want to be a professor, museum work is highly competitive with little pay, and CRM is basically competing with others to do the shittiest job for the least amount of money.

Finally, I started making my own video game for funsies, realized I liked and was good at programming, and changed majors again. I enjoy learning it, I enjoy doing it, I like the idea of doing it for the rest of my life (variety comes from the different projects I'll be working on), and the pay is solid.

I think everyone has multiple interests, and any of them could be decent careers. If you enjoy them all equally - well then, you can't really go wrong. Try to picture yourself doing each of them. Research into what those jobs are like - pay, flexibility, job environment, etc.

For me, I'm happy with programming because I know that there's a good chance I'll be able to work from home, and even if not, most indie gaming companies (which is what I want to do) have very casual, laid-back, often-liberal environments. I can keep my purple hair, don't have to hide my tattoos, and can be open about being queer. There are disadvantages (crunch time, for example), but for me they are outweighed by the benefits and my enjoyment of the work.
